title: Leadership Advice That Sounds Good But Will Destroy You
author: The Good Boss
summary: Gaurav Jain argues that some popular leadership advice is like a beautifully wrapped empty gift: attractive, widely quoted, and harmful when taken literally. He examines six maxims, my door is always open, you do not need to be liked just respected, empower your team and get out of the way, lead with vulnerability, treat everyone the same, and celebrate failure. For each he explains the failure mode, such as silence when the burden of approaching a powerful boss falls on the team, or performative learning when failure is celebrated. He then gives a better practice, such as walking out of the open door, pairing warmth with competence, giving clarity rather than control, and treating people equitably. The closing test is to ask whether the advice will help this team, in this context, right now.
points: An open-door policy puts the whole burden on the team, so leaders should proactively check in and use one-on-ones to surface what goes unsaid.
Leading only through respect produces obedience without openness, whereas warmth and competence together build trust and influence.
Empowerment without direction, support or feedback becomes absence and silent chaos.
Vulnerability should serve the team's needs, with mistakes and lessons shared but emotional burdens not handed to the team.
Celebrate learning rather than failure, otherwise teams start failing to look bold.
quotes: Don’t just have an open door, walk out of it. Proactively check in with your team members, ask them thoughtful questions… make them feel like you actually care.
When you lean only on respect, you lead with authority. And when you lead with authority, your team may “obey”, but they won’t really open up.
I’ve seen leaders say this… and then disappear. They provide no direction, no support, and no feedback.
Give your team clarity, not control. Set clear goals, share the ‘why’, and empower them to own the path.
Be real and authentic, but always serve the team’s needs, not your own. Admit mistakes, share what you learned, but don’t make your team carry your emotional burden.
Treat people equitably, not equally. Adjust to the individual. Be consistent in your values, but flexible in how you lead.
Celebrate learning, not failure. Show that risk-taking is okay when it leads to some learning and helps your team to improve.
